newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity in lawsuit with Magellan Fund shareholder.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity in lawsuit with Magellan Fund shareholder.

text.p: A stockholder of Fidelity Investments' Magellan Fund claims he is out of as much as $2.5 million after the mutual fund giant allegedly lost his address and turned his account over to the state.
Fidelity, the nation's largest mutual fund company, said in its defence that it complied with the laws in handling the account and it not legally required to ante up the missing funds.
The dispute has landed in the hands of the Suffolk County Superior Court in Boston.
Maurice Barron, a retired advertising executive from Randolph, Mass., invested $500 in Magellan in 1965 in an account in his infant son Sean's name, according to court documents.
In 1969, the family moved across town, and Barron informed Fidelity of his new address, where he then received numerous mailings concerning other Fidelity funds over the years.
In 1986, when Sean turned 21, his father gave him his original Magellan certificate, which used to be issued to fund investors to verify ownership.
He and his father received telephone calls in 1994 from a person describing themselves as an investigator, who told them that the Magellan account had been turned over to the state in 1982.

Fidelity claimed in court documents that it had received three returned pieces of mail it had sent to Sean's address, and therefore turned the fund over to the state in accordance with adandoned properties laws.
But Fidelity has not been able to produce evidence of the three pieces of mail and Justice Richard Chin struck those claims from court records.
Moreover, Fidelity had Sean's and his father's address and social security numbers in their records in connection with other mutual funds, according to court documents.

Sean appealed to Fidelity and the state, and received checks totalling $104,000 from Massachusetts, which Fidelity said was the value of the fund when it was sold by the state in 1988 plus statutory interest.

His lawyer Colette Manoil has asked Fidelity to calculate the current value of the account if it had remained invested. Fidelity has refused, saying in court records that there is no legal basis for a defendant to calculate damages for the plaintiff.
Despite Magellan's well-publicised recent performance problems, the $54 billion fund was one of the best performing mutual funds throughout the 1980s.

Manoil said that using figures supplied by Fidelity, the account could be worth anywhere from $750,000 to $2.5 million. Sean Barron, now 31 and a father of two young children, was in a boating accident last year and has stopped working as an emergency medical technician since then due to his injuries, Manoil said.
Fidelity said the account would have been worth much less, only $172,575 as of December, 1994.
Fidelity denied allegations that it breached its fiduciary duty since, according to state laws, it had no fiduciary duty with the Barron's in the matter.

Nevertheless, Fidelity has offered to settle the case out of court and pay Sean Barron $105,621, the difference between the Dec., 1996 value of the fund and the amount he already received from the state, spokesman Scott Beyerl said.

"We have offered to make the shareholder completely whole, by paying in full what his shares in Magellan would have been had he remained in the fund," Beyerl said. "We thought it would be appropriate in this case to accomodate the shareholder in this fashion."
The Barron's have refused and are seeking a jury trial and punitive damages.
"The money is not the issue. What Fidelity is telling us now is that you invest with Fidelity at your own peril," Manoil told Reuters.
A Suffolk County Superior Court Judge will hear a motion by Fidelity on Feb. 24 to dismiss the case.
